DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Odido lookalike Okta/SSO phishing-portal domain resolution (ShinyHunters vishing) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts DNS/network connections to attacker-registered lookalike domains that impersonate Odido's SSO, IT-support, or Okta login pages — the AiTM portals ShinyHunters (UNC6661/UNC6671) directs vished employees to. Because the lure arrives by phone/SMS out-of-band, network/DNS telemetry (not corporate email) is the detection surface. Rationale: Applies Huntress-documented ShinyHunters lookalike-domain naming convention (<company>sso[.]com, <company>okta[.]com, <company>support[.]com, <company>internal[.]com, <company>access[.]com) to 'odido'; vishing delivers the link out-of-band so DNS/network egress is the correct pivot rather than EmailEvents. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/threat-actors/shinyhunters • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://socradar.io/blog/major-cyber-attacks-february-2026/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1656 T1598.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team sandboxing/analysing the phishing domain (SOC investigation traffic)
  • Brand-monitoring / takedown vendors resolving lookalike domains on the org's behalf
  • Third-party marketing microsite legitimately using an odido- prefixed domain
  • Typo of odido.nl resolving via a parked/registrar landing page
Suppression filter
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("odido.nl","odido.com")) and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host/user and whether a browser process reached the domain; pull the Okta/Entra sign-in for that user in the following 15 min to confirm a session was established. 2) Contain: block the domain at DNS/proxy, force-revoke the user's SSO sessions/tokens and reset credentials + re-enroll MFA. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the same domain list, review Okta system log for failure-burst-then-success and new MFA factor enrollment on that account, and check for SSO-burst app access.
let lookalikes = dynamic(["odidosso","odido-sso","myodidosso","odidosupport","odido-support","support-odido","odidookta","odido-okta","odidointernal","odido-internal","odidoaccess","odido-access","odidoazure"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (lookalikes)
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("odido.nl","odido.com"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookalikes = dynamic(["odidosso","odido-sso","myodidosso","odidosupport","odido-support","support-odido","odidookta","odido-okta","odidointernal","odido-internal","odidoaccess","odido-access","odidoazure"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (lookalikes)
| where not(DnsQuery has_any ("odido.nl","odido.com"))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DvcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Odido Lookalike Okta/SSO Phishing Domain Resolution
id: 8f2b1c44-3d6e-4a9f-9c2a-6e1d0b7a5f31
description: Detects DNS queries to lookalike domains impersonating Odido SSO/IT-support/Okta portals used by ShinyHunters (UNC6661/UNC6671) AiTM vishing.
references:

  - https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign

date: 2026/07/10
tags:

  - attack.t1656

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(*odidosso* OR *odido-sso* OR *myodidosso* OR *odidosupport* OR *odido-support* OR *support-odido* OR *odidookta* OR *odido-okta* OR *odidointernal* OR *odidoaccess* OR *odidoazure*) -@DestinationHostname:(*odido.nl OR *odido.com)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/odido-?(sso|support|okta|internal|access|azure)/i
| NOT DomainName=/odido\.(nl|com)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query IN ("*odidosso*","*odido-sso*","*myodidosso*","*odidosupport*","*odido-support*","*support-odido*","*odidookta*","*odido-okta*","*odidointernal*","*odido-internal*","*odidoaccess*","*odido-access*","*odidoazure*")) AND NOT (DNS.query IN ("*odido.nl","*odido.com")) by DNS.query DNS.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query IN ("*odidosso*","*odido-sso*","*myodidosso*","*odidosupport*","*odido-support*","*support-odido*","*odidookta*","*odido-okta*","*odidointernal*","*odido-internal*","*odidoaccess*","*odido-access*","*odidoazure*")) AND NOT (DNS.query IN ("*odido.nl","*odido.com")) by DNS.query DNS.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| sort - lastTime
ShinyHunters Okta AiTM: failure-heavy auth flow then success (~10 min) AIExploitation High
Detects the ShinyHunters/UNC6661 adversary-in-the-middle signature in Okta logs: a prolonged, failure-heavy authentication sequence (policy.evaluate_sign_on, app.ad.login.bad_password, core.user.factor.attempt_fail) that ends in a successful session for the same user within a short window — the fingerprint of an operator relaying credentials/MFA through a phishing proxy. Rationale: Uses the exact Okta event names Obsidian documented for this campaign (policy.evaluate_sign_on, app.ad.login.bad_password, core.user.factor.attempt_fail) plus the observed ~10-minute failure-then-success cadence, which distinguishes AiTM relay from a normal fat-finger login. Cross-checked against: • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://www.intel471.com/blog/shinyhunters-0-day-attacks-after-patching-find-out-if-you-were-breached
ATT&CKT1621 T1111 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User genuinely forgetting password / fumbling MFA push before succeeding
  • Password rotation day producing repeated app.ad.login.bad_password before cache refresh
  • Flaky mobile network causing multiple factor.attempt_fail before a legit push accept
  • New device onboarding where the user retries several factors
Suppression filter
| where Failures >= 5 and Successes >= 1 and LastSuccess > FirstFail and array_length(SrcIPs) >= 1
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the src IP/ASN and user-agent of the successful session — check for a datacenter/residential-proxy ASN and emulated-Android UA. 2) Contain: revoke all Okta sessions/OAuth tokens for the user, force password reset and MFA re-enrollment, and quarantine any newly enrolled factor. 3) Hunt: check whether a new 'Passkey' MFA device was enrolled right after the success, and whether the account then burst-accessed multiple SSO apps or downloaded bulk SaaS files.
ImAuthentication
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventProduct has "Okta"
| summarize Failures = countif(EventResult == "Failure"),
            Successes = countif(EventResult == "Success"),
            FirstFail = minif(TimeGenerated, EventResult == "Failure"),
            LastSuccess = maxif(TimeGenerated, EventResult == "Success"),
            SrcIPs = make_set(SrcIpAddr, 10)
        by TargetUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where Failures >= 5 and Successes >= 1   // ~10-min failure-heavy AiTM flow ending in success (baseline P99 fail-then-success <=2)
| where LastSuccess > FirstFail
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:okta @outcome.result:FAILURE @evt.name:(policy.evaluate_sign_on OR core.user.factor.attempt_fail OR app.ad.login.bad_password)
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count(eval(Authentication.action="failure")) as failures count(eval(Authentication.action="success")) as successes min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app="okta" by Authentication.user Authentication.src _time span=15m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where failures >= 5 AND successes >= 1
| eval flowSeconds=lastTime-firstTime
| where flowSeconds <= 900
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count(eval(Authentication.action="failure")) as failures count(eval(Authentication.action="success")) as successes min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app="okta" by Authentication.user Authentication.src _time span=15m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where failures >= 5 AND successes >= 1
| eval flowSeconds=lastTime-firstTime
| where flowSeconds <= 900
| sort - lastTime
Rogue Okta MFA factor enrolled as 'Passkey' from Genymobile-emulated Android AIInstallation High
Detects ShinyHunters' MFA-persistence step: enrolling an Okta Verify/FastPass factor on an emulated Android device consistently named 'Passkey' with the user-agent com.okta.android.auth/8.19.0 running under Genymobile. This is a high-fidelity, campaign-specific string set rather than generic 'new MFA device' noise. Rationale: Anchored to three corroborated, high-specificity strings from Obsidian/Huntress — the 'Passkey' device name, the Genymobile emulator, and the exact com.okta.android.auth/8.19.0 build — so it fires almost exclusively on this actor's MFA-hijack step. Cross-checked against: • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/threat-actors/shinyhunters
ATT&CKT1556.006 T1098.005
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • QA/security team using a Genymobile emulator to test Okta mobile enrollment
  • Developer legitimately naming a passkey factor 'Passkey' on a physical device (UA will differ)
  • MDM bulk re-enrollment campaign touching user.mfa.factor.update at scale
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the enrollment's src IP/UA and whether it followed a failure-burst login for the same user. 2) Contain: delete the rogue factor, revoke all sessions/tokens, reset credentials and re-enroll MFA on a verified device; disable the account if access spread. 3) Hunt: enumerate all factors enrolled from Genymobile UAs or named 'Passkey' across the tenant, and review SSO-burst / bulk-download activity from the affected accounts.
title: Rogue Okta MFA Enrollment - Passkey Device on Genymobile Emulator (ShinyHunters)
id: 2c7d9a10-5b4e-4f21-8ad3-1e6c9b2f7a44
description: Detects Okta MFA factor enrollment on an emulated Android device named 'Passkey' with the com.okta.android.auth/8.19.0 Genymobile user-agent, matching ShinyHunters (UNC6661/UNC6671) persistence.

Post-compromise SSO burst: single account rapidly accessing many SaaS apps AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the ShinyHunters 'SSO burst' behavior where a hijacked identity enumerates and authenticates into an unusually large number of SSO-connected applications within minutes to locate data repositories. Distinct pivot from the auth-failure UC: this counts distinct downstream apps per account in a tight window. Rationale: Directly implements the 'rapid access to an unusual number of SSO-connected applications' / 'SSO Burst' behavior documented by Obsidian and Intel 471 for this campaign, counting distinct downstream apps per identity per 10-minute bin. Cross-checked against: • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://www.intel471.com/blog/shinyhunters-0-day-attacks-after-patching-find-out-if-you-were-breached
ATT&CKT1538 T1528 T1078.004

Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Onboarding/offboarding automation or an IdP admin testing app assignments
  • A power user (exec/IT) who legitimately touches many apps at start of day
  • SSO session-refresh storm after a certificate/metadata rotation reissuing tokens for all apps
  • Scripted health-check / synthetic monitoring account probing multiple SaaS apps
Suppression filter
| where AppCount >= 8 and not(AccountDisplayName has_any ("svc-","sync","automation","admin-onboard"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the app list and src IP — flag if apps span unrelated business units (CRM + storage + chat) from one IP/UA. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/tokens, reset credentials, and step-up MFA; temporarily restrict the account to essential apps via conditional access. 3) Hunt: pivot to bulk-download activity in the accessed apps (Salesforce Data Loader, SharePoint/Drive/Slack exports) and to the preceding rogue MFA enrollment.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType has_any ("LoggedIn","Login","Logon","SignIn")
| summarize AppCount = dcount(Application), Apps = make_set(Application, 30), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
        by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where AppCount >= 8   // rapid SSO fan-out; typical user P99 <=4 distinct apps / 10m
| order by AppCount desc
ImAuthentication
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventProduct has "Okta" and EventResult == "Success"
| summarize AppCount = dcount(TargetAppName), Apps = make_set(TargetAppName, 30), SrcIPs = make_set(SrcIpAddr, 10)
        by ActorUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where AppCount >= 8   // SSO burst threshold; baseline P99 <=4 distinct apps / 10m
| order by AppCount desc
source:okta @evt.name:user.authentication.sso @outcome.result:SUCCESS
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true dc(Authentication.app) as appCount values(Authentication.app) as apps values(Authentication.src) as srcs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action="success" Authentication.vendor_product="Okta" by Authentication.user _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where appCount >= 8
| sort - appCount
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Authentication.app) as appCount values(Authentication.app) as apps values(Authentication.src) as srcs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action="success" Authentication.vendor_product="Okta" by Authentication.user _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where appCount >= 8
| sort - appCount
Bulk SaaS data exfil: high-volume automated downloads (Salesforce/SharePoint/Drive/Slack) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the ShinyHunters exfiltration stage — a hijacked account pulling a very large number of files within a sustained window (Obsidian observed ~90-minute automated download sessions and downloads seconds apart), plus PowerShell-driven SharePoint/OneDrive bulk downloads on the endpoint. Matches the 88GB / 15M-record theft profile from the Odido breach. Rationale: Implements Obsidian's documented exfil signature — high-volume downloads within seconds over a ~90-minute automated session across Google Drive/Slack/SharePoint plus PowerShell SharePoint/OneDrive pulls — matching Odido's disclosed 88GB / 15M-record theft. Cross-checked against: • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://socradar.io/blog/major-cyber-attacks-february-2026/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1530 T1213
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate large migration / eDiscovery / backup export by IT
  • Employee bulk-downloading their own project folder before leaving or for offline work
  • OneDrive/SharePoint sync client doing a full re-sync after cache reset
  • Data-science pipeline account exporting datasets on schedule
Suppression filter
| where Downloads >= 100 and WindowSec <= 5400 and not(AccountDisplayName has_any ("backup","svc-","migration","ediscovery"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the account, src IP/app, and whether downloads span sensitive repositories (CRM/customer-contact data); check if PowerShell UA or Salesforce Data Loader was involved. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/tokens, block the src IP, disable the account, and preserve the download logs for scope. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the rogue MFA enrollment and SSO burst for the same identity, and check for the account leaving internal security Slack channels or extortion email from shinycorp@tutanota.com / shinygroup@onionmail.com.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType has "Download"   // FileDownloaded, FileSyncDownloadedFull, FileDownloadedFromSharePoint
| summarize Downloads = count(), Apps = make_set(Application, 10), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstDl = min(Timestamp), LastDl = max(Timestamp)
        by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| extend WindowSec = datetime_diff('second', LastDl, FirstDl)
| where Downloads >= 100 and WindowSec <= 5400   // >=100 files inside a <=90-min automated pull
| order by Downloads desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Operation in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileSyncDownloadedPartial")
| summarize Downloads = count(), DistinctFiles = dcount(SourceFileName), FirstDl = min(TimeGenerated), LastDl = max(TimeGenerated)
        by UserId, ClientIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m)
| extend WindowSec = datetime_diff('second', LastDl, FirstDl)
| where Downloads >= 100 and WindowSec <= 5400   // >=100 files inside a <=90-min automated pull
| order by Downloads desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(sharepoint\.com|-my\.sharepoint\.com|graph\.microsoft\.com|onedrive)/i
| CommandLine=/(Invoke-WebRequest|iwr|DownloadFile|Start-BitsTransfer|Invoke-RestMethod)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
index=o365 Operation IN ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileSyncDownloadedPartial")
| bin _time span=30m
| stats count as downloads dc(SourceFileName) as distinctFiles values(ClientIP) as ips min(_time) as firstDl max(_time) as lastDl by UserId _time
| eval windowSeconds=lastDl-firstDl
| where downloads >= 100 AND windowSeconds <= 5400
| sort - downloads
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

URGENT - Progress Tells ShareFile Customers to Shut Down Storage Zone Controllers Over Security Threat

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 9 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Progress Software has told ShareFile customers to shut down the Windows servers running their Storage Zone Controllers, confirming to The Hacker News that it is responding to a "credible external security threat." The company has temporarily disabled access to the affected accounts, a step it says it took "out of an abundance of caution" while it works with internal and external security

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ShareFile Storage Zone Controller pre-auth exploit URIs in IIS logs (CVE-2026-2699/2701)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ShareFile Storage Zone Controller IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawns shell/recon child · [LLM] ASPX webshell written under ShareFile Storage Zone Controller storage path · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
ShareFile Storage Zone Controller pre-auth exploit URIs in IIS logs (CVE-2026-2699/2701) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the specific ShareFile Storage Zone Controller endpoints abused in the watchTowr-disclosed pre-auth RCE chain: the ConfigService auth-bypass page, the misspelled StroageZoneConfig API, and upload.aspx with an unzip parameter. This is the exact initial-access signature behind Progress's shutdown order. Rationale: Uses the exact exploit endpoints from watchTowr's chain writeup — /ConfigService/Admin.aspx (auth bypass), the misspelled /ConfigService/api/StroageZoneConfig, and upload.aspx?...unzip. The typo'd internal API path is effectively pathognomonic for exploitation. IIS logs are the only telemetry carrying the URI, so Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch are left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/youre-not-supposed-to-sharefile-with-everyone-progress-sharefile-pre-auth-rce-chain-cve-2026-2699-cve-2026-2701/ • https://watchtowr.com/resources/progress-sharefile-storage-zone-controller-pre-auth-rce-cve-2026-2699-cve-2026-2701/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/progress-urges-sharefile-customers-to-shut-down-servers-over-credible-threat/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Qualys/Tenable/Rapid7) probing the same endpoints
  • watchTowr / Shadowserver internet-wide exposure scans hitting /ConfigService
  • Legitimate ShareFile admin reaching /ConfigService/Admin.aspx from an internal management IP after authenticating
  • Security team replaying PoC during authorized IR validation
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("<internal_vuln_scanner_ip>") // suppress authorized scanner ranges; keep external IPs in scope
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all hits for the offending cIP; check scStatus — a 200/302 on /ConfigService/Admin.aspx or a POST to upload.aspx?...unzip from an external IP is a likely successful exploit, and requests to the misspelled StroageZoneConfig confirm PoC-derived tooling. 2) Contain: per Progress guidance, keep the controller offline; block the source IP at the perimeter and preserve IIS logs and the storage tree for forensics. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to newly written .aspx files under \StorageCenter\ (UC2) and w3wp.exe child shells (UC3); scope the source IP across all internet-facing assets.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/ConfigService/Admin.aspx", "/ConfigService/api/StroageZoneConfig", "/documentum/upload.aspx")
   or (csUriStem endswith "/upload.aspx" and csUriQuery has "unzip")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SrcIP = cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, UserAgent = csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ShareFile Storage Zone Controller IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawns shell/recon child AIInstallation High
Detects the post-exploitation execution stage of the ShareFile pre-auth RCE: the IIS worker process hosting the Storage Zone Controller (w3wp.exe) spawning interactive shells or host-recon binaries, which is how an uploaded ASPX webshell runs commands. Directly supports the article's 'treat it as a possible incident' guidance. Rationale: w3wp.exe (the IIS worker) spawning cmd/powershell/recon binaries is the direct execution artifact of an ASPX webshell running commands on the Storage Zone Controller — the exact chain outcome watchTowr demonstrated. Parent=w3wp + child shell/LOLBin is the high-fidelity pair; scope to ShareFile SZC hosts via the FP filter to cut other IIS app pools. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/youre-not-supposed-to-sharefile-with-everyone-progress-sharefile-pre-auth-rce-chain-cve-2026-2699-cve-2026-2701/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2023/08/17/cve-2023-24489-exploited/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/progress-sharefile-admins-shut-down-servers/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Other IIS-hosted web apps on the same server legitimately shelling out (custom .NET apps calling Process.Start)
  • Web app deployment/maintenance running appcmd, DISM, or provisioning scripts under w3wp
  • Monitoring/APM agents invoking cmd or PowerShell from the worker
  • Admin troubleshooting an app pool via a diagnostic .aspx page
  • Backup or config tooling that shells out during app-pool recycle
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("StorageCenter", "documentum", "ShareFile") // restrict to the ShareFile SZC app pool; drop to widen to all IIS
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child — whoami/net/nltest recon or download strings (certutil/bitsadmin/curl) launched by w3wp on a ShareFile host is near-certain webshell RCE; capture the full process tree and parent w3wp command line (app-pool name). 2) Contain: isolate the host and keep the controller offline per Progress guidance; snapshot memory before reboot to preserve any in-memory implant. 3) Hunt: correlate to newly written .aspx under \StorageCenter\ (UC3) and inbound exploit URIs (UC1) within the preceding minutes; sweep for outbound connections from w3wp and new local accounts/services.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","ipconfig.exe","systeminfo.exe","nltest.exe","hostname.exe","tasklist.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","reg.exe","sc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe", @"\net.exe", @"\net1.exe", @"\whoami.exe", @"\ipconfig.exe", @"\systeminfo.exe", @"\nltest.exe", @"\hostname.exe", @"\tasklist.exe", @"\cscript.exe", @"\wscript.exe", @"\certutil.exe", @"\bitsadmin.exe", @"\reg.exe", @"\sc.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ASPX webshell written under ShareFile Storage Zone Controller storage path AIInstallation High
Detects creation of ASPX/ASHX web-executable files inside the Storage Zone Controller's IIS-served storage tree (…\StorageCenter\…\files\ul-…), which is where the CVE-2026-2699/2701 chain drops its webshell. This is the persistence artifact Progress told admins to look for ('unfamiliar .aspx files in the web folders and storage paths'). Rationale: watchTowr confirmed the webshell lands under the SZC storage location that overlaps the IIS web root (e.g. C:\inetpub\wwwroot\ShareFile\StorageCenter\documentum\files\ul-<id>\1\). A newly created .aspx/.ashx under any \StorageCenter\ path is the article's 'unfamiliar .aspx' artifact — legitimate ShareFile user uploads are documents, not server-executable pages in that tree. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/youre-not-supposed-to-sharefile-with-everyone-progress-sharefile-pre-auth-rce-chain-cve-2026-2699-cve-2026-2701/ • https://support.sharefile.com/s/article/ShareFile-StorageZones-Controller-Security-Update-for-CVE-2023-24489 • https://docs.sharefile.com/en-us/storage-zones-controller/5-0/security-vulnerability-feb26.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Progress-signed installer/upgrade writing legitimate .aspx pages during a 5.12.4 patch deployment
  • Admin manually placing a diagnostic or health-check .aspx in the StorageCenter web app
  • A user legitimately uploading a document literally named *.aspx into a ShareFile storage zone (rare)
  • Backup/restore tooling re-creating the StorageCenter directory tree
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe", "ShareFile.StorageCenter.Setup.exe", "TrustedInstaller.exe") // exclude signed installer/patch writes; investigate w3wp.exe-authored files
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve and read the file contents/hash — webshell indicators are eval/Request/Process.Start/cmd handlers; check InitiatingProcess (w3wp.exe writing it is damning) and creation time against the patch-deployment window. 2) Contain: keep the controller offline per Progress; quarantine the file, preserve a copy for forensics, and block the uploading source IP. 3) Hunt: pivot to inbound exploit URIs (UC1) and w3wp child shells (UC2) near the file-creation time; hash-sweep all SZC hosts for the same file and scan every internet-facing controller for .aspx under \StorageCenter\.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has @"\StorageCenter\"
| where FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".ashx" or FileName endswith ".asmx" or FileName endswith ".asp"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\StorageCenter\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("aspx", "ashx", "asmx", "asp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Injective Labs GitHub Compromise Pushes Wallet-Key-Stealing npm Packages

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 13 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Unknown threat actors compromised the Injective Labs SDK project's GitHub repository and leveraged it to publish a malicious package on the npm registry to steal cryptocurrency wallet private keys and mnemonic seed phrases. The compromised version, @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21, came embedded with fake telemetry functionality that exfiltrated data from cryptocurrency wallets. The version was

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Install/pin of malicious @injectivelabs ...@1.20.21 supply-chain version in package manager cmdline
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 artifact by SHA256 on developer/CI endpoints · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Wallet-key exfil beacon to Injective SDK C2 host testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Wallet-key exfil beacon to Injective SDK C2 host testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound DNS/HTTPS to the exact attacker subdomain that the trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 uses to POST stolen private keys and mnemonics. The host is shaped to blend with real Injective gRPC-web infra but this specific FQDN is attacker-controlled and appears only in the malicious build. Rationale: The FQDN testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network is the single hard-coded exfil endpoint confirmed by Socket, Aikido and OX Security; it never appears in legitimate Injective SDK traffic, making an exact-match resolution/connection a near-zero-FP signal. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/compromised-injective-sdk-npm-package • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-injectivelabs-exfiltrates-keys • https://www.ox.security/blog/injectivelabs-npm-package-hijacked-impacting-87-dependent-packages/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/injective-sdk-on-npm-infected-with-cryptocurrency-wallet-stealer/
ATT&CKT1041 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox tooling actively resolving the IOC for validation
  • SOAR/EDR auto-detonation of the flagged package in a lab detonation host
  • Security researcher reproducing the attack in an isolated build
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the blocked lookup
  • Passive-DNS collector replaying historical resolutions
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sandbox_detonator.exe","threatintel-resolver.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user and the process that opened the connection (Node.js/CI runner) and confirm @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 is present in that project's node_modules/lockfile. 2) Contain: block the FQDN at DNS/proxy, isolate the developer/CI host, and treat every private key or mnemonic ever handled on that host as compromised — force wallet key/seed rotation immediately. 3) Hunt: pivot on the two malicious artifact SHA256s across all endpoints and CI, enumerate all 18 pinned @injectivelabs@1.20.21 packages and transitive dependents, and search for prior beacons to the host over the full retention window.

Trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 artifact by SHA256 on developer/CI endpoints AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the on-disk presence of the two known-malicious release artifacts of the compromised Injective SDK build, which remained downloadable from GitHub even after npm deprecation. High-fidelity because it keys on published file hashes, not behavior. Rationale: Keys on the two SHA256 artifact hashes published for the compromised build (still hosted on GitHub after npm deprecation); a file-hash match is deterministic and requires no behavioral inference. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/compromised-injective-sdk-npm-package • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-injectivelabs-exfiltrates-keys
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis/repro workstation intentionally holding the sample
  • EDR quarantine or forensic evidence store retaining the file
  • Security team distributing the IOC bundle internally for testing
  • Backup/snapshot restore surfacing an old node_modules copy
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "\\Quarantine\\" and FolderPath !has "\\malware-samples\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hash hit is within a live project (node_modules/cache) versus a quarantine/analysis path, and identify the owning developer/CI job. 2) Contain: remove/upgrade to clean @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.23, purge npm caches, and rotate every wallet private key/mnemonic that transited that host. 3) Hunt: enumerate all 18 @injectivelabs@1.20.21 pinned packages and transitive dependents in lockfiles org-wide, and correlate with any beacon to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network.

Install/pin of malicious @injectivelabs ...@1.20.21 supply-chain version in package manager cmdline AIDelivery Medium
Hunts npm/yarn/pnpm invocations that install or pin the poisoned 1.20.21 version of the Injective SDK or its 17 sibling wallet packages, catching the compromise at install time even when the artifact hash has been rebuilt. Article-specific to the exact malicious version string and scoped package names. Rationale: Combines the scoped package prefix @injectivelabs/ with the exact malicious version 1.20.21 (Socket/OX Security list all 18 packages pinned to that version); the clean release is 1.20.23, so a 1.20.21 pin in a package-manager cmdline is a strong install-time indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ox.security/blog/injectivelabs-npm-package-hijacked-impacting-87-dependent-packages/ • https://socket.dev/blog/compromised-injective-sdk-npm-package
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer intentionally pinning 1.20.21 for repro/forensics before remediation
  • CI pipeline replaying an old lockfile that still references 1.20.21
  • Dependency-scanning tool echoing the version string in its own command line
  • Internal advisory script that greps for the bad version by name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "dependency-scan" and ProcessCommandLine !has "--dry-run"
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the command actually installed (exit success, node_modules populated) versus a scan/echo, and identify the repo and user. 2) Contain: bump the dependency to 1.20.23 across affected repos, invalidate CI caches, and rotate any wallet secrets exercised on that runner/host. 3) Hunt: sweep all lockfiles/package.json for @injectivelabs@1.20.21 and transitive pins, then correlate hosts with the C2-domain and artifact-hash detections.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "@injectivelabs/" and ProcessCommandLine has "1.20.21"
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm","yarn","pnpm")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "@injectivelabs/" and CommandLine has "1.20.21"
| where CommandLine has_any ("npm","yarn","pnpm","node")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Install of Poisoned Injective SDK Version 1.20.21
id: 8c3d6b02-1f45-4a7e-9d18-0b2e6a94f7c5
description: Package-manager command line installing or pinning the malicious @injectivelabs 1.20.21 supply-chain version.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/injective-labs-github-compromise-pushes.html
  - https://www.ox.security/blog/injectivelabs-npm-package-hijacked-impacting-87-dependent-packages/

  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:

detection:

source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @CommandLine:(*@injectivelabs/* AND *1.20.21*)

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*@injectivelabs/*" AND Processes.process="*1.20.21*" AND (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npm-cli.js","npx.exe") OR Processes.process="*npm*" OR Processes.process="*yarn*" OR Processes.process="*pnpm*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-2699", "CVE-2026-2701")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-2699", "CVE-2026-2701")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33243")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33243")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High

Laser Attack Resets Tangem Wallet Passwords on Cards That Can't Be Patched

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 6 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Researchers at Ledger's&nbsp;Donjon security team&nbsp;have shown that a precisely timed laser pulse, aimed at the chip inside a Tangem crypto wallet card, can reset the card's password to anything the attacker picks. No old password. No backup card. Once it is reset, whoever did it controls the wallet and can move the coins&nbsp;out. This is not an emergency for most owners. The attack needs

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
