| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Researcher Details WhatsApp-to-Host Attack Chain Using Three OpenClaw Flaws

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Details have emerged about three now-patched security flaws in the OpenClaw personal artificial intelligence (AI) assistant that, if successfully exploited, could enable credential theft, privilege escalation, and arbitrary code execution on the host. A brief description of the high-severity vulnerabilities is as follows&nbsp;- GHSA-hjr6-g723-hmfm (CVSS score: 8.8) - An operating system

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Git ext:: external transport helper command execution (OpenClaw WhatsApp-to-host RCE) · [LLM] Container bind-mount of parent /home or /var (OpenClaw denylist parent-directory bypass) · [LLM] Docker socket access by non-Docker process (OpenClaw /var mount host escape)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Single process reading multiple users' SSH/AWS/GPG secrets under /home (OpenClaw mount harvest) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Git ext:: external transport helper command execution (OpenClaw WhatsApp-to-host RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts git clone/fetch/remote invocations whose URL uses the ext:: transport helper, which lets an attacker-supplied string run an arbitrary OS command as the process user. The OpenClaw advisories and the researcher explicitly recommend monitoring for git 'ext::' as the RCE primitive reachable from an external WhatsApp message. Rationale: The article and the OpenClaw maintainers name 'ext::' as the exact string to monitor; git's ext:: transport is a documented arbitrary-command primitive (Snyk SNYK-JS-SIMPLEGIT-3112221, GitHub advisory GHSA-r275-fr43-pm7q), so a git command line containing 'ext::' is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://git-scm.com/docs/git-remote-ext • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-SIMPLEGIT-3112221 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r275-fr43-pm7q
ATT&CKT1059 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately testing a custom git-remote-ext transport helper
  • CI/CD tooling that wraps git over a bespoke ext:: transport (rare)
  • Security researcher reproducing the CVE in a lab on the same fleet
  • Automated migration scripts that pipe git through an ext:: proxy command
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code","jetbrains","pycharm") and AccountName !in~ ("jenkins","gitlab-runner")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and decode the ext:: payload (everything after 'ext::' is the command that ran); identify the parent process — if it is the OpenClaw gateway/agent binary rather than an interactive shell, treat as confirmed exploitation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the OpenClaw agent session, and rotate any credentials reachable from the process (SSH, cloud, GPG). 3) Hunt: on the same host look for follow-on bind-mounts of /home or /var and any docker.sock access (see companion UCs); confirm OpenClaw is upgraded to 2026.6.6 and 'exec' is removed from channel-facing tool allowlists.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "ext::"
| where FileName =~ "git" or ProcessCommandLine has "git"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "ext::"
| where ActingProcessName has "git" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "git"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Container bind-mount of parent /home or /var (OpenClaw denylist parent-directory bypass) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts container/mount commands that bind-mount the whole /home or /var directory into a container. GHSA-575v-8hfq-m3mc lets a source path escape the bind-mount denylist by mounting the parent of a blocked dir, exposing every user's ~/.ssh, ~/.aws and ~/.gnupg (via /home) or the Docker socket (via /var). Rationale: Uses the article's exact bypass mechanic (mounting parent /home or /var instead of the blocked ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.gnupg subdirs). Mounting an entire top-level dir into a container is rare in legit ops, so scoping to /home:/var roots keeps fidelity high. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.quarkslab.com/why-is-exposing-the-docker-socket-a-really-bad-idea.html • https://github.com/portainer/portainer/security/advisories/GHSA-7fw3-x4r2-g7wc
ATT&CKT1610 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup jobs that bind-mount /home read-only into a backup container
  • Monitoring/agent containers that mount /var/log or /var (over-broad ops config)
  • Developer running a build container with -v /home:/host for convenience
  • Log-shipping sidecars mounting /var for journald access
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has ":ro" and AccountName !in~ ("backup","veeam","root-cron")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the mount source is the top-level /home or /var (not a scoped subdir) and identify the container image and the invoking user/process; a mount driven by the OpenClaw gateway is confirmed abuse. 2) Contain: stop and remove the offending container, unmount the bind, and rotate SSH/AWS/GPG material for any user under the exposed /home. 3) Hunt: check for subsequent docker.sock interaction (host escape) and cross-user credential file reads on the same host; verify OpenClaw is on 2026.6.6 with sandbox mode enabled for non-main sessions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("docker","podman","nerdctl","runc","mount")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-v /home:","-v /var:","--volume /home:","--volume /var:","source=/home,","source=/var,","--bind /home ","--bind /var ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("docker","podman","nerdctl","runc","mount")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-v /home:","-v /var:","--volume /home:","--volume /var:","source=/home,","source=/var,","--bind /home ","--bind /var ")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Container Bind-Mount of Parent /home or /var (OpenClaw Denylist Bypass)
id: 1d4f8a22-6c9b-4e73-a5d1-2f0b7c9e4a11
description: Detects docker/podman/mount commands bind-mounting the whole /home or /var directory into a container, the parent-directory bypass of GHSA-575v-8hfq-m3mc that exposes SSH/AWS/GPG secrets and the Docker socket.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/researcher-details-whatsapp-to-host.html
  - https://blog.quarkslab.com/why-is-exposing-the-docker-socket-a-really-bad-idea.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:
  - attack.t1610
  - attack.t1611
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/docker'
      - '/podman'
      - '/nerdctl'
      - '/runc'
      - '/mount'
  selection_mount:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '-v /home:'
      - '-v /var:'
      - '--volume /home:'
      - '--volume /var:'
      - 'source=/home,'
      - 'source=/var,'
      - '--bind /home '
      - '--bind /var '
  condition: selection_img and selection_mount
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.name:(docker OR podman OR nerdctl OR runc OR mount)) AND (@process.command_line:(*"-v /home:"* OR *"-v /var:"* OR *"source=/home,"* OR *"source=/var,"* OR *"--bind /home "* OR *"--bind /var "*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\/(docker|podman|nerdctl|runc|mount)$/i
| CommandLine=/(-v |--volume |source=|--bind )\/(home|var)[:, ]/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("docker","podman","nerdctl","runc","mount")) AND (Processes.process="*-v /home:*" OR Processes.process="*-v /var:*" OR Processes.process="*--volume /home:*" OR Processes.process="*--volume /var:*" OR Processes.process="*source=/home,*" OR Processes.process="*source=/var,*" OR Processes.process="*--bind /home *" OR Processes.process="*--bind /var *") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("docker","podman","nerdctl","runc","mount")) AND (Processes.process="*-v /home:*" OR Processes.process="*-v /var:*" OR Processes.process="*--volume /home:*" OR Processes.process="*--volume /var:*" OR Processes.process="*source=/home,*" OR Processes.process="*source=/var,*" OR Processes.process="*--bind /home *" OR Processes.process="*--bind /var *") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Docker socket access by non-Docker process (OpenClaw /var mount host escape) AIExploitation High
Hunts non-Docker binaries (curl, socat, python, shell) interacting with /var/run/docker.sock. After the /var parent-directory bind-mount bypass, an attacker reaches the Docker socket from inside the sandbox and achieves full host escape by driving the Docker API. Rationale: The article states mounting /var yields the Docker socket and 'full host escape from inside the sandbox.' A non-docker binary referencing docker.sock (esp. curl --unix-socket / socat) is the canonical escape and is near-zero-FP outside DevOps tooling. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.quarkslab.com/why-is-exposing-the-docker-socket-a-really-bad-idea.html • https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/security/advisories/GHSA-w235-x559-36mg
ATT&CKT1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portainer/Watchtower/Traefik containers legitimately calling the Docker API via curl-like clients
  • CI runners that use socat to proxy docker.sock
  • Sysadmin one-off `curl --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock`
  • Docker Compose helper scripts invoking the API over the socket
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("portainer","watchtower","traefik") and AccountName !in~ ("jenkins","gitlab-runner")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and determine whether the caller is a sanctioned management container (Portainer/Watchtower) or an ephemeral sandbox process spawned from the OpenClaw agent; the latter is confirmed escape. 2) Contain: kill the process, isolate the host, and snapshot for forensics before the attacker pivots via the Docker API (new privileged containers, host root mounts). 3) Hunt: enumerate containers created/started around the event, check for -v /:/host or --privileged spawns, and review the OpenClaw gateway session that triggered it; patch to 2026.6.6.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "docker.sock"
| where FileName !in~ ("docker","dockerd","containerd","podman")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--unix-socket","unix://","/containers/","/exec","socat","curl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "docker.sock"
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("docker","dockerd","containerd","podman")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--unix-socket","unix://","/containers/","/exec","socat","curl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Docker Socket Access by Non-Docker Process (OpenClaw Host Escape)

Single process reading multiple users' SSH/AWS/GPG secrets under /home (OpenClaw mount harvest) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts one process opening credential files (~/.ssh keys, ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.gnupg) belonging to more than one /home user in a short window — the exfiltration signature of the OpenClaw /home bind-mount bypass, which the researcher says lets you 'read every user's SSH keys, AWS credentials, and GPG secrets.' Rationale: Directly encodes the researcher's stated impact — one container process reading multiple users' ~/.ssh, ~/.aws and ~/.gnupg via the /home mount. Keying on >=2 distinct /home users separates targeted cross-user harvest from a user touching their own keys. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/security/advisories/GHSA-w235-x559-36mg
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Configuration-management agent (Ansible/Salt) reading multiple users' authorized_keys during a run
  • Backup software archiving /home
  • Migration/imaging tooling copying user profiles between hosts
  • Central SSH key-rotation script iterating over /home users
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","salt-minion","puppet","rsync","tar","restic","borg")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and whether it runs inside an OpenClaw sandbox/container; a single short-lived process reading >2 users' private keys and cloud creds is confirmed harvest. 2) Contain: isolate the host and immediately revoke/rotate every exposed SSH key, AWS access key, and GPG key; invalidate cloud sessions minted from those creds. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent bind-mount of /home (companion UC) and any outbound transfer of the collected files; audit AWS CloudTrail for use of the leaked access keys from new source IPs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath startswith "/home/"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.ssh/", "/.aws/", "/.gnupg/")
| where FileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519","id_ecdsa","id_dsa","credentials") or FolderPath has "/.gnupg/"
| extend HomeUser = extract(@"/home/([^/]+)/", 1, FolderPath)
| summarize DistinctHomeUsers = dcount(HomeUser), Users = make_set(HomeUser, 20), Files = make_set(FolderPath, 50), FileCount = count() by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DistinctHomeUsers >= 2
| order by DistinctHomeUsers desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/home/"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.ssh/", "/.aws/", "/.gnupg/")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519","id_ecdsa","id_dsa","credentials") or TargetFilePath has "/.gnupg/"
| extend HomeUser = extract(@"/home/([^/]+)/", 1, TargetFilePath)
| summarize DistinctHomeUsers = dcount(HomeUser), Users = make_set(HomeUser, 20), Files = make_set(TargetFilePath, 50) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessCommandLine, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctHomeUsers >= 2
| order by DistinctHomeUsers desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*\/home\/* AND (*.ssh\/id_* OR *.aws\/credentials* OR *.gnupg\/*)) AND @process.name:(cat OR tar OR cp OR scp OR base64 OR gpg)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| TargetFileName=/\/home\/[^\/]+\/\.(ssh\/id_|aws\/credentials|gnupg\/)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true))
| _count >= 3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(Filesystem.file_path) as distinct_secret_files values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="/home/*/.ssh/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/home/*/.aws/credentials" OR Filesystem.file_path="/home/*/.gnupg/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where distinct_secret_files >= 3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - distinct_secret_files
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Filesystem.file_path) as distinct_secret_files values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="/home/*/.ssh/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/home/*/.aws/credentials" OR Filesystem.file_path="/home/*/.gnupg/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user

| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

MODBEACON scheduled-task persistence pointing to user-writable path AIInstallation Medium
Hunts MODBEACON's persistence step where the separated loader/beacon registers a scheduled task whose action points to a binary staged in a user-writable path (AppData/Temp/Public/Downloads/ProgramData) after a counterfeit SEO-poisoned installer runs. Article-specific because it pairs schtasks /create with the temp/user staging paths MODBEACON's memory-resident loader drops into, rather than the Program Files paths legitimate installers use. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit 'setting persistence using scheduled tasks' plus the memory-resident loader staging in user-writable/temp paths rather than Program Files; no second source corroborated MODBEACON IOCs (search returned only Xray/V2Ray project pages confirming the gRPC transport it reuses exists), so this is behaviour-based and safe to ship without IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/xtls/xray-core
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software updaters (Google/Edge/Adobe) that stage in ProgramData/AppData and register update tasks
  • Portable apps run from Downloads that self-register a scheduled task
  • IT deployment/RMM tooling creating tasks from a temp staging directory
  • Developer/build tooling scripting schtasks /create from a temp workspace
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("googleupdate.exe","microsoftedgeupdate.exe","officeclicktorun.exe","msiexec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full schtasks /create command line and the task action path; inspect the parent process (InitiatingProcess) — confirm whether it descends from a recently downloaded installer/ZIP and whether the target binary is signed. 2) Contain: if the action binary is unsigned and in a user-writable path, disable/delete the task (schtasks /delete), isolate the host, and quarantine the referenced binary. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for outbound HTTPS beaconing to Amazon/Cloudflare CDN from non-browser processes and for the originating counterfeit-installer ZIP in Downloads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Scheduled Task Persistence Pointing to User-Writable Path (MODBEACON)
id: 6f2b1c94-0a7d-4d3e-9c2a-8f1e5b3a7c11
description: Detects schtasks.exe creating a scheduled task whose action references a binary in a user-writable path, consistent with MODBEACON loader/beacon persistence.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-modbeacon-rat-uses-grpc-streaming.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '/create'
  paths:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\Public\'
      - '\Downloads\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
  condition: selection and paths
level: medium
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE OR *\Schtasks.exe) @CommandLine:(*create*) @CommandLine:(*\AppData\* OR *\Temp\* OR *\Public\* OR *\Downloads\* OR *\ProgramData\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/\/create/i
| CommandLine=/\\(AppData|Temp|Public|Downloads|ProgramData)\\/i
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName, ParentImageFileName])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe AND Processes.process="*/create*" AND (Processes.process="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Public\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\ProgramData\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe AND Processes.process="*/create*" AND (Processes.process="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Public\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\ProgramData\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | sort - lastTime
MODBEACON gRPC/CDN heartbeat beaconing from non-browser user-path process AICommand & Control Low
Hunts MODBEACON's encrypted gRPC-over-HTTP/2 C2 heartbeats fronted by Amazon and Cloudflare CDN, surfacing non-browser processes running from user-writable paths that make sustained, regular outbound HTTPS connections. Article-specific because it targets the memory-resident beacon (payload staged by a counterfeit installer, not an installed app) exhibiting periodic heartbeat cadence to CDN infrastructure rather than normal browsing. Rationale: Targets the article's headline behaviour — encrypted gRPC/HTTP2 heartbeat C2 fronted by Amazon/Cloudflare CDN — by combining the memory-resident beacon's user-writable staging path, a non-browser initiator, and sustained regular-cadence egress; kept as a hunt because no C2 domains/IPs were published (only the QiAnXin-sourced THN article, corroborated only for the Xray/V2Ray gRPC transport it reuses). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/xtls/xray-core
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573.002 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Auto-updaters/telemetry agents staged in ProgramData beaconing to CDN endpoints
  • Electron or portable apps run from Downloads polling a CDN-hosted API
  • EDR/RMM agents in ProgramData with regular check-in cadence to cloud infrastructure
  • Software licensing/heartbeat services legitimately hosted behind CloudFront/Cloudflare
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessSHA256 !in ((DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory | summarize by SHA256="")) or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sensendr.exe","msmpeng.exe","googleupdate.exe","microsoftedgeupdate.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating binary (hash, path, signer) and check whether it is a known application; review the connection interval regularity and whether the destination is Cloudflare/CloudFront fronting an otherwise unknown domain. 2) Contain: if the binary is unsigned/memory-resident with no install footprint, isolate the host and block the destination IP/domain at the proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: look for a sibling scheduled-task persistence entry (UC1), host-fingerprinting discovery commands immediately preceding first beacon, and the counterfeit-installer ZIP source in Downloads.
let Browsers = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (443, 80)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (Browsers)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Public\", @"\Downloads\")
| extend IsCdn = tostring(RemoteUrl) has_any ("cloudfront.net","amazonaws.com","cloudflare","cdn")
| summarize ConnCount=count(), DistinctMinutes=dcount(bin(Timestamp,1m)), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Remotes=make_set(RemoteUrl,10), AnyCdn=max(IsCdn) by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteIP
| where DistinctMinutes >= 20 and ConnCount >= 40
| order by ConnCount desc

| where DistinctMinutes >= 20 and ConnCount >= 40
| order by ConnCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:(443 OR 80) @Image:(*\AppData\* OR *\Temp\* OR *\ProgramData\* OR *\Public\* OR *\Downloads\*) -@Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\firefox.exe OR *\brave.exe OR *\iexplore.exe OR *\opera.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=443

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Critical

Unpatched XRING Flaw in XQUIC Lets Remote Clients Crash HTTP/3 Servers

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A single wrong variable on one line in XQUIC, Alibaba's QUIC and HTTP/3 library, lets any remote client crash the server with a short burst of completely legal traffic. There is no patch. FoxIO researcher Sébastien Féry&nbsp;disclosed the flaw on July 8&nbsp;and nicknamed it XRING. He says it needs no login and no malformed packets: about 260 bytes of ordinary QPACK traffic takes the server

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Tengine/XQUIC HTTP/3 worker crash-loop via glibc fortify abort (XRING DoS) · [LLM] Tengine/nginx HTTP/3 worker respawn storm (XRING crash-loop symptom) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Tengine/XQUIC HTTP/3 worker crash-loop via glibc fortify abort (XRING DoS) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts repeated aborts/segfaults of the Tengine or XQUIC-linked HTTP/3 worker process in Linux syslog. The XRING QPACK ring-buffer overflow is caught by glibc _FORTIFY_SOURCE=2, which prints 'buffer overflow detected' and raises SIGABRT (signal 6); repeated occurrences on an HTTP/3 front-end indicate the ~260-byte QPACK DoS being replayed rather than a one-off bug. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete crash mechanism (glibc _FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 -> 'buffer overflow detected'/SIGABRT) plus the named vulnerable software (XQUIC/libxquic, Tengine). The QUIC payload is encrypted on the wire, so the server-side abort signature is the only reliable telemetry; a repeat threshold separates a DoS replay from an incidental crash. No CIM datamodel covers process-crash syslog, so SPL is a raw index search. Cross-checked against: • https://www.penligent.ai/hackinglabs/cve-2026-42530-2/ • https://github.com/alibaba/xquic • https://socprime.com/blog/cve-2026-42530-critical-nginx-http-3-flaw-can-trigger-dos-and-possible-rce/
ATT&CKT1499.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated nginx/Tengine third-party module segfault after an upgrade
  • OOM-killer terminating a worker under memory pressure (SIGKILL, not SIGABRT — usually excluded by message tokens)
  • Disk-full or config-parse abort during deploy
  • A genuine but non-malicious QPACK/HTTP-3 stability bug hit by a real client
  • Fuzzing/pentest activity from an authorized internal scanner
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "Out of memory" and SyslogMessage !has "oom-kill" and SyslogMessage !has "emerg" and SyslogMessage !has "could not open"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full syslog lines on the affected host; confirm the process is the HTTP/3 front-end (Tengine/xquic) and that the crash message is a fortify/SIGABRT overflow, then check whether the site listens on UDP/443 with http3 enabled and QPACK dynamic table on. 2) Contain: apply the vendor workaround — set SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY to 0 (disables the QPACK dynamic table) or disable HTTP/3 on the listener until a fixed XQUIC release ships. 3) Hunt: pivot to firewall/QUIC flow logs for the source IPs sending short (~260-byte) UDP/443 bursts immediately before each crash, and check other Tengine/XQUIC front-ends for the same crash signature.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ProcessName in~ ("tengine","nginx","xquic") or SyslogMessage has_any ("tengine","nginx","xquic","libxquic")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("buffer overflow detected","stack smashing detected","segfault","signal 6","SIGABRT","general protection")
| summarize CrashCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleMsg = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, ProcessName
| where CrashCount >= 3   // 3+ HTTP/3 worker aborts in 24h = likely XRING replay, not a one-off crash
| order by CrashCount desc
source:linux.syslog (@process.name:(tengine OR nginx) OR *xquic* OR *libxquic*) (*"buffer overflow detected"* OR *"stack smashing detected"* OR *segfault* OR *"signal 6"* OR *SIGABRT*)
APPLICATION
index=os OR index=linux sourcetype IN ("linux_messages_syslog","syslog") (process=tengine OR process=nginx OR "xquic" OR "libxquic") ("buffer overflow detected" OR "stack smashing detected" OR "segfault" OR "signal 6" OR "SIGABRT" OR "general protection")
| stats count as CrashCount min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen values(_raw) as SampleMsg by host
| where CrashCount>=3
| sort - CrashCount
Tengine/nginx HTTP/3 worker respawn storm (XRING crash-loop symptom) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the process-creation side of the XRING DoS: after each worker aborts, the Tengine/nginx master rapidly forks replacement 'worker process' children. An abnormally high count of worker respawns in a short window on an HTTP/3 front-end indicates the server is being crash-looped, and is visible even when the fortify message format differs or syslog isn't collected. Rationale: Targets the named vulnerable servers (Tengine, nginx) via the 'worker process' command line and a respawn-rate threshold — the observable secondary effect of the XRING abort loop. Distinct pivot from UC1 (process creation vs syslog crash message) so it fires on EDR telemetry even without syslog collection. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/alibaba/xquic • https://socprime.com/blog/cve-2026-42530-critical-nginx-http-3-flaw-can-trigger-dos-and-possible-rce/
ATT&CKT1499.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Planned config reload (SIGHUP) draining and forking workers during a deploy
  • Autoscaling / container restarts spinning up many nginx instances at once
  • Log-rotation reopen triggering worker cycling
  • A high worker_processes count on first boot after a host reboot
  • Legitimate high-traffic reload storms behind a CI/CD pipeline
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "reload" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "-s reload"
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged host, confirm the respawns are unscheduled — check for a concurrent config reload/deploy in change management and correlate with UC1's crash signature in the same window. 2) Contain: if no change window matches, treat as active DoS — apply the SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY=0 workaround or disable HTTP/3 on the listener. 3) Hunt: sweep all internet-facing Tengine/XQUIC hosts for the same respawn pattern and pull QUIC/UDP-443 flow logs for the source IPs driving the short bursts preceding each respawn spike.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(6h)
| where FileName in~ ("nginx","tengine")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "worker process"
| summarize WorkerSpawns = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Host = any(DeviceName) by DeviceId, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where WorkerSpawns >= 10   // steady-state nginx/tengine rarely respawns workers; 10+ in 5m = crash-loop
| order by LastSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(6h)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("nginx","tengine")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "worker process"
| summarize WorkerSpawns = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where WorkerSpawns >= 10
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(nginx OR tengine) @process.command_line:*"worker process"*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(nginx|tengine)$/i CommandLine=/worker process/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(as=spawns))
| spawns >= 10
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("nginx","tengine") AND Processes.process="*worker process*") by Processes.dest, _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where count>=10
| rename count as WorkerSpawns
| sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("nginx","tengine") AND Processes.process="*worker process*") by Processes.dest, _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where count>=10
| rename count as WorkerSpawns
| sort - _time

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'

falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-42530")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-42530")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-42530")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-42530")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Nacos auth bypass via spoofed 'Nacos-Server' User-Agent (CVE-2021-29441) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] WordPress/Joomla webshell (down.php / BestShell) written by web-server account · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] VShell backdoor masquerading as Linux kernel thread [kworker/0:2] · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Web-server process spawning shell/recon binaries (webshell command execution) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
VShell backdoor masquerading as Linux kernel thread [kworker/0:2] AICommand & Control High
Hunts the WP-SHELLSTORM crew's remote-access implant: a userland process that renames itself to the kernel-thread name [kworker/0:2] to blend into the process list, dropped in-memory by the SNOWLIGHT loader (memfd_create). Legitimate kernel worker threads never have a backing on-disk/mem image or a real command line, so a 'kworker' process with a genuine executable path is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the article's exact masquerade string '[kworker/0:2]' for the VShell implant; kernel threads never carry a real executable path, so the FolderPath/ImageFileName present + kworker name is a near-zero-FP tell. Corroborated by Sysdig and Trellix write-ups of the SNOWLIGHT→VShell chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/unc5174-chinese-threat-actor-vshell • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/the-silent-fileless-threat-of-vshell/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/04/chinese-hackers-target-linux-systems.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom monitoring/HPC agents that intentionally name worker processes 'kworker-*'
  • Container runtimes spawning short-lived helper procs with kworker-like names
  • Security tooling that itself references 'kworker' in a scan command line
  • Developer scripts grepping for kworker in process names (command line contains the token but is benign)
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/var/tmp/","/run/","/home/","memfd") or FolderPath startswith "/proc/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the true FolderPath/SHA256 of the flagged process; a path in /tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp or a memfd:/deleted image confirms masquerade. Check parent process for a SNOWLIGHT-style loader. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory before kill (payload is fileless), block egress to unknown remote IPs the process holds. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SHA256/parent across the fleet, review web-server logs on the host for the exploited plugin CVE that led to code exec, and sweep for down.php webshells.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "kworker" or FileName has "kworker"
| where isnotempty(FolderPath) and FolderPath !startswith "["
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "kworker"
| where isnotempty(ActingProcessName) and ActingProcessName !startswith "["
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: VShell Backdoor Masquerading as Kernel Worker Thread

description: Detects a userland Linux process masquerading as a [kworker] kernel thread, a defense-evasion technique used by UNC5174 VShell.

  - attack.t1620

Nacos auth bypass via spoofed 'Nacos-Server' User-Agent (CVE-2021-29441) AIDelivery High
Hunts the crew's earlier corporate-Java campaign that skipped Nacos authentication by sending the User-Agent 'Nacos-Server' to config endpoints, then pulled 613 config files (AWS/Alibaba/Oracle keys, DB passwords, Alipay RSA keys). Any HTTP request carrying that exact User-Agent against /nacos/ paths is exploitation, not normal traffic. Rationale: The User-Agent string 'Nacos-Server' is the exact backdoor value CVE-2021-29441 keys on (isEnableUserAgentAuthWhite), scoped to /nacos/ config/admin paths named in the advisory — legitimate clients never send it externally. Cross-checked against GitHub Security Lab GHSL-2020-325 and Tenable's CVE-2021-29441 plugin. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylab.github.com/advisories/GHSL-2020-325_326-nacos/ • https://www.tenable.com/plugins/nessus/154416
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate intra-cluster Nacos node-to-node sync (real Nacos servers do send this UA — scope to external/untrusted source IPs)
  • Internal blue-team vulnerability scanners testing CVE-2021-29441
  • Nuclei/nessus template runs that replay the Nacos-Server UA
  • Load balancer health checks that were mis-configured to spoof the UA
Suppression filter
| where not (ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "10.0.0.0/8") or ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "172.16.0.0/12") or ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, "192.168.0.0/16"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is external/untrusted (internal Nacos peer sync legitimately uses this UA); check RequestURL for /cs/configs read or /auth/users add. 2) Contain: rotate EVERY credential stored in the Nacos config (cloud keys, DB passwords, RSA keys) — not just the obvious ones — set nacos.core.auth.enabled=true and upgrade to >=1.4.1/2.2.1. 3) Hunt: review outbound connections from the Nacos host, look for follow-on config exfil and any pivot into cloud accounts using the leaked keys.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where RequestClientApplication == "Nacos-Server"
| where RequestURL has "/nacos/"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WordPress/Joomla webshell (down.php / BestShell) written by web-server account AIInstallation High
Hunts the plant step of WP-SHELLSTORM: the exploited plugin (Breeze CVE-2026-3844, Joomla JCE CVE-2026-48907, etc.) causes the web-server user to write a PHP webshell — the crew's primary backdoor is named down.php, a 4-layer-obfuscated BestShell derivative. A .php file created inside web root by www-data/apache/nginx/php-fpm is the signature of a webshell drop. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named backdoor 'down.php' plus the generic 'web-server user writes .php into web root' shape; the web-server account writing new PHP is rarely legitimate outside of plugin/theme updates. The exact filename branch is alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/exposed-hacker-server-reveals-wp.html
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WordPress/Joomla plugin or theme auto-updates writing PHP files
  • WP-CLI or composer deployments run as the web-server user
  • Caching plugins (including Breeze itself) generating .php cache files
  • CMS core updates unpacking new .php files into web root
  • Developer staging deployments run under the apache/nginx account
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-cli","composer","apt","yum","dpkg") or FolderPath has_any ("/cache/","/wp-content/cache/","/tmp/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the flagged file — 4-layer obfuscation / eval/gzinflate/base64 chains or BestShell markers confirm webshell; check FolderPath is inside web root. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, take a copy for IR, pull access logs for the URL of the shell and block the source IPs; patch the exploited plugin (Breeze 2.4.5, JCE 2.9.99.5). 3) Hunt: search for the web-server process spawning /bin/sh (command execution via the shell), and for a VShell [kworker] implant indicating deeper access.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "down.php" or (FileName endswith ".php" and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","http","daemon","php-fpm"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php","php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName =~ "down.php" or (TargetFileExtension =~ "php" and ActorUsername in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","httpd","http","daemon"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web-server process spawning shell/recon binaries (webshell command execution) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts hands-on-keyboard use of the down.php webshell: php-fpm/apache/nginx spawning a shell or recon utility (sh, id, whoami, uname, curl, wget). The BestShell-derived backdoor runs commands, opens reverse shells, and checks which security software is present — all of which surface as a web-server parent spawning a non-PHP child. Rationale: Targets the article's description of down.php running commands / opening reverse shells / enumerating security software — expressed as the web-server parent → shell/recon child process tree, a pivot distinct from the file-write UC. Behaviourally scoped so it is not the generic 'Office spawns script' pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/exposed-hacker-server-reveals-wp.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PHP apps that legitimately shell out (image processing via ImageMagick convert, PDF generation, git/composer hooks)
  • Monitoring plugins invoking uname/id for host info
  • Backup scripts triggered by the web app calling curl/wget
  • CI deploy hooks run under the web-server user
  • Health-check endpoints that exec whoami/uname
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","gs ","ghostscript","composer","git ","/backup/") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: read ProcessCommandLine of the child — recon (id;uname;whoami), a reverse shell (bash -i, nc -e), or a download (curl/wget to an unknown IP) confirms webshell use; identify the parent PHP file. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process chain, block the remote IP, and quarantine the identified webshell (likely down.php). 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceFileEvents for the webshell write, look for a VShell [kworker] implant on the same host, and review whether cloud/DB credentials on the host were accessed.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'

            - '\mspub.exe'

level: high

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'

    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args

      cross-shell escaping
level: high
